content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper describes the distributed acoustic sensing problem in fluid flow settings and casts it as a continual learning problem. It proposes the multi-step cutout data augmentation strategy for training the model, where several boxes are randomly placed in an image and the corresponding pixels are set to 0. It is then paired with an inverse cutout compression strategy, which takes isolated patches from the image and chooses the one with the highest cross-entropy to represent that image. This is used within a memory-based continual learning model. The proposed approach outperforms baseline approaches on a real-world DAS dataset, and on continual-learning versions of MNIST and CIFAR-10.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
- DAS seems like an interesting and challenging problem that pushes the limits of existing techniques due to the high volume of data.
- The multi-step cutout and inverse cutout techniques are very simple and appear to be effective.

Weaknesses
- DAS needs to be better described. I have a high-level understanding, but a figure would really be more clarifying than the current description of the problem. The specific data especially in terms of what is being fed to the ML model.
- Based on my understanding, it's unclear if continual learning is appropriate for the DAS setup. My understanding is that DAS is a regression problem, and that these values are binned in order to turn it into a classification problem. It doesn't make sense to me from a time-series prediction perspective to split those classes randomly into different tasks. Rather, it seems like a problem where one would want to keep all 72 bins per task, but where the bin distribution changes as time goes on.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The paper should be as self-contained as possible. This includes describing the blurry-n setup in more detail, as referencing Bang et al. was unnecessarily time consuming.
- It's unclear if training the CL model is a two-step process, or if multi-step cutout followed by inverse cutout are interleaved for each task? That is, do you train the CL model on several tasks, then go back and compress them, or do you train on a task, compress the task, train on the next task, compress that task, and so on?
content.summary_of_the_review:
DAS seems like a new and interesting domain for continual learning. The proposed multi-step cutout and inverse-cutout techniques are extremely simple. So much so that I would be skeptical of their effectiveness on continual learning in general. However, there are experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 that show that these techniques are quite effective. Moreover, it does seem like they work outside of the domain of natural images.

However, I don't understand why DAS itself makes sense as a continual learning problem. It seems to me that DAS is a regression problem, where the distribution over inputs and outputs changes over time. The paper frames DAS as a classification problem by binning the values of the output, forming 72 classes, but then I don't quite see why it would make sense for tasks to contain some output values and not others. Could the authors please explain to me why this is a continual learning problem that conforms to the blurry-N setting and not a domain adaptation problem, or online learning where all classes appear in each task?

I also don't know what the current approaches for DAS are. How do neural networks stack up compared to what is in use today? If you train a predictive model on available data, and then deploy it, how quickly does it degrade without adaptation? Is 32% accuracy good, or do we still have a long way to go to make these practical? All of the DAS metrics that I could see are in the context of comparing continual learning approaches, meaning I don't have an absolute sense of how well these methods work.

DAS makes up a large portion of the paper. Otherwise, there are experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 that are very promising, but would not alone be able to convincingly justify the proposed strategies. If the authors could provide more clarity and motivation for DAS, then I would consider raising my score.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper uses Continual Learning to accurately estimate flow characteristics in fluid pipelines. The authors propose a compression method to address the memory bottleneck in consuming a considerable amount of input sensory data.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- This work addresses a real-world application.
- Probably introduces a new type of signal that has received less attention in prior work.


Weaknesses:
- The machine learning contributions might seem marginal in the current draft. Memory-intensive inputs have been faced before in other applications such as Lidar and 3D sensings. Does the introduced method extend to other applications as well? If so, it'd be nice to see the evaluations for other signal modalities as well. 
- The paper mentions using continual learning to improve the test-time accuracy, but in its current form, it neither convinced me that CL is the only way of doing this task nor it showed a complete comparison against strawman baselines. For example, what happens if we train a huge offline model?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper's clarity looks acceptable to me. Though, if the key novelty is the data augmentation method, maybe it could be written around that instead of starting from the continual learning constraints.  

The work seems original, but the novelties might look incremental to the ML community.
content.summary_of_the_review: I understand that this can be an application paper, but at least the achieved results in their current form might be more appreciated if submitted to a venue more related to the task it's trying to solve. For a machine learning venue, this requires establishing a more thorough connection to the prior work in this area.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a continual learning method to solve the fluid flow estimation problem in the Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) problem. The model will be continued to be trained when implemented. Due to the fact that the traditional CL approach is unsuitable for the DAS problem, which has more OOD events than the standard CL tasks, the authors proposed a compressed CL method based on the memory-bank-based method to solve the DAS problem. This paper proposed a compression algorithm to store more representative data and thus improve performance. Some experiment results indicate that the proposed method is effective and achieved SOTA results on the Mnist and CIFAR-10 datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
1. The paper is well-organized.
2. The DAS problem is a good application of CL. 

Cons:
1. Cifar 10 and Mnist are not convincing as the CL benchmark, as their classes are too fewer. Besides, the baselines are too weak to be compared with,  for example, RMN and CPG. They have achieved 81% and 80.9% acc on the CIFAR-100 dataset; it is doubtful that 77.27% is the SOTA result of the CIFAR-10.  
2. The background section should be more concise. It is better not to repeat too much about CL. Place more emphasis on the novel part of your method. 
3. The authors should introduce their novelty/method more in the introduction. There are only three lines to talk about that. 
4. There is no reference to the Figures in this paper. The figures are not related to the text.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The novlery of this paper is limited. It is more like a combination of cutout and CL method. The evluation is not convising. And the SOTA results is hard to be consider as the front-tier performance.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed method of this paper is more like a simple combination of Cutout and memory-bank-based CL methods. The experimental results are not convincing as the DAS datasets and CIFAR-10 are not the widely-used benchmarks for CL.

content.title: Towards Realtime Distributed Virtual Flow Meter via Compressed Continual Learning
content.abstract: A robust-accurate estimation of fluid flow is the main building block of a distributed virtual flow meter. Unfortunately, a big leap in algorithm development would be required for this objective to come to fruition, mainly due to the inability of current machine learning algorithms to make predictions outside the training data distribution. To improve predictions outside the training distribution, we explore the Continual Learning (CL) paradigm for accurately estimating the characteristics of fluid flow in pipelines. A significant challenge facing CL is the concept of catastrophic forgetting. In this paper, we provide a novel approach of how to address the forgetting problem via compressing the distributed sensor data to increase the capacity of CL memory bank using a compressive learning algorithm. Through extensive experiments, we show that our approach provides around 8% accuracy improvement compared to other CL algorithms in the real-field distributed sensor dataset. Noticeable accuracy improvement is also achieved when using our proposed approach with the CL-benchmark datasets, achieving state-of-the-art accuracies of 94.95% and 77.27% for the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, respectively.
